summary.text: Climate change feedbacks are natural processes that affect how much global temperatures rise for a given amount of greenhouse gas emissions.
Positive feedbacks amplify warming and negative ones diminish it, and the labels say nothing about whether a feedback is good or bad.
Their overall sum is negative, mostly because a warmer planet gives off more thermal radiation, but it is becoming less negative as emissions continue.

facts.label: CO₂ taken up yearly
facts.value: More than half of emissions, by plants and ocean

items.prompt: Warming melts snow and ice, leaving a less reflective surface, and that region then warms even more. How is this feedback classified?
items.explain: A feedback that amplifies the initial change is positive; reduced snow and ice cover is one of the feedbacks behind polar amplification.

items.prompt: Why can human-caused climate change not, on its own, set off a runaway greenhouse effect?

options.label: Emissions will run out of fuel
A warmer Earth radiates more heat away

items.explain: Extra thermal radiation from a warmer planet is several times larger than any other single feedback, keeping the net feedback negative.

items.prompt: The atmosphere warms by a degree. What happens to its water vapor, and what does that do?

options.label: Vapor rises and adds more warming
Vapor falls and cools the air
Vapor rises and cools the air
Vapor stays the same either way

items.explain: Warmer air can hold more water vapor, and because vapor is a greenhouse gas, that warms the air further.

items.prompt: A news report calls a newly found climate feedback 'positive'. What does that word tell you about it?

options.label: It is good news for the planet
It has been proven by observation

items.explain: In this context positive means it enhances warming; the name implies nothing about whether it is good or bad.

items.prompt: Plants and the ocean now soak up more than half of each year's CO₂ emissions. Over the long term, what is expected to happen to that share?

options.label: It grows as plants get bigger
It shrinks as sinks fill up
It jumps once ice sheets melt

items.explain: Carbon sinks become saturated and higher temperatures bring drought and wildfires, reducing the percentage absorbed.

items.prompt: Climate scientists separate feedbacks from forcings. Which of these is a natural external forcing?
items.explain: External forcings come from outside the climate system, and volcanic eruptions are a natural example; the others are responses within it.
